title: Errors
notes:
What is an Error in Measurement?

Every measurement involves some uncertainty. The difference between the measured value and the true (actual) value of a physical quantity is called the error. No measurement is perfectly accurate because instruments have finite precision, observers have limited senses, and environmental conditions fluctuate. A complete measurement result must include both a value and its uncertainty: Measurement = Measured value \pm Error, e.g., area = 200 \pm 0.2 cm² means the true value lies between 199.8 and 200.2 cm².

Types of Errors

Errors are broadly classified into Systematic errors (repeatable, predictable, same direction) and Random errors (unpredictable, varying in magnitude and direction). Gross errors are mistakes due to carelessness (wrong reading, calculation error) and should be avoided. Systematic errors include instrumental errors (zero error, calibration error), personal errors (parallax error), and environmental errors (temperature, humidity, pressure variations). Random errors arise from unpredictable fluctuations in experimental conditions and observer judgment.

Systematic Errors — Causes and Correction

Instrumental errors: Every measuring device has limitations. A worn-out meter stick, a spring scale that hasn't been zeroed, or a Vernier caliper with backlash are common causes. These are corrected by calibration against a standard. Personal (observational) errors: Parallax error occurs when the eye is not directly in line with the scale marking. Minimized by using mirrors behind needles (as in Vernier calipers). Environmental errors: Temperature changes cause thermal expansion/contraction of instruments and specimens. Humidity affects electrical measurements. These are minimized by controlling lab conditions or applying correction factors.

Random Errors — Statistical Treatment

Random errors cannot be predicted for a single measurement, but they follow statistical patterns over many trials. If you make n measurements A₁, A₂, ..., A_n, the arithmetic mean \bar{A} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} A_i is the best estimate of the true value. The absolute error for each measurement is \Delta A_i = \bar{A} - A_i. The mean absolute error \overline{\Delta A} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} |\Delta A_i| gives the average magnitude of random errors. The relative error is \overline{\Delta A}/\bar{A}, and percentage error is (\overline{\Delta A}/\bar{A}) × 100%. As n increases, the mean absolute error decreases as 1/\sqrt{n}, so repeated measurements improve precision.

Significant Figures

Significant figures are the digits in a measurement that are known reliably plus one estimated digit. Rules: (1) All non-zero digits are significant. (2) Zeros between non-zero digits are significant (e.g., 1003 has 4 sig figs). (3) Leading zeros are NOT significant (e.g., 0.00356 has 3 sig figs). (4) Trailing zeros after a decimal point ARE significant (e.g., 0.07600 has 4 sig figs). (5) Trailing zeros in a whole number without a decimal are ambiguous (3400 may have 2, 3, or 4 sig figs; use scientific notation: 3.400 × 10³ for 4 sig figs). (6) Exact numbers (counts, definitions) have infinite significant figures.

Rules for Arithmetic Operations with Significant Figures

Addition/Subtraction: The result should have the same number of decimal places as the term with the FEWEST decimal places. Example: 10.3 + 2.45 = 12.75 → 12.8 (one decimal place, limited by 10.3). Multiplication/Division: The result should have the same number of significant figures as the term with the FEWEST significant figures. Example: 2.5 × 3.42 = 8.55 → 8.6 (2 sig figs, limited by 2.5). Note: These rules are approximate; the full treatment uses error propagation (see below).

Error Propagation in Addition and Subtraction

When quantities are added or subtracted, the absolute errors add. For x = a + b or x = a - b: \Delta x = \Delta a + \Delta b. The maximum relative error in the sum or difference is not simply related to individual relative errors. Example: If A = (10.0 \pm 0.2) cm and B = (5.0 \pm 0.1) cm, then A + B = (15.0 \pm 0.3) cm and A - B = (5.0 \pm 0.3) cm. The absolute error in the result is the SUM of the absolute errors of individual measurements.

Error Propagation in Multiplication and Division

When quantities are multiplied or divided, the relative errors add. For x = a \times b or x = a/b: \frac{\Delta x}{x} = \frac{\Delta a}{a} + \frac{\Delta b}{b}. For powers: if x = a^n, then \frac{\Delta x}{x} = n \cdot \frac{\Delta a}{a}. Example: Volume of sphere V = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3. If the error in r is 1%, then \frac{\Delta V}{V} = 3 \times 1\% = 3%. Example: Density \rho = m/V. If error in m is 2% and in V is 1%, then \frac{\Delta \rho}{\rho} = 2\% + 1\% = 3%.

Accuracy vs. Precision

Accuracy measures how close a measured value is to the TRUE value. An accurate measurement has small systematic error. Precision measures how close repeated measurements are to each other (reproducibility). A precise measurement has small random error. A measurement can be precise but inaccurate (consistent but biased), accurate but not precise (scattered around true value), both, or neither. Example: Target analogy — all shots near bullseye = accurate + precise; clustered off-center = precise but inaccurate; scattered around bullseye = accurate on average but imprecise.

Least Count Error

The least count of an instrument is the smallest value it can measure. For a Vernier caliper, LC = 1 MSD - 1 VSD = 0.01 cm; for a screw gauge, LC = pitch/number of divisions = 0.001 cm. The least count error is the uncertainty associated with the smallest division — it sets a fundamental limit on accuracy. The reading is always uncertain by \pm half the least count (\pm 0.005 cm for Vernier caliper). Using instruments with smaller least count increases precision.
confusion: Significant figures are NOT the same as decimal places — 4.00 has 3 significant figures AND 2 decimal places; 0.004 has 1 significant figure BUT 3 decimal places; always count from the first non-zero digit.

Error is NOT the same as mistake — A mistake (gross error) is a blunder like misreading the scale or wrong calculation; it should be discarded. Error is the inherent uncertainty in every measurement and must be reported.

Absolute error and relative error measure DIFFERENT things — Absolute error \Delta x tells you the size of uncertainty in the original units; relative error \Delta x/x tells you the uncertainty as a fraction of the measurement, useful for comparing precision across different scales.

When multiplying, add relative errors; when adding, add absolute errors — This is a common mix-up. For x = ab: \Delta x/x = \Delta a/a + \Delta b/b (relative errors). For x = a + b: \Delta x = \Delta a + \Delta b (absolute errors).

A dimensionless quantity CAN have significant figures — Refractive index 1.33 has 3 significant figures; a percentage like 98.5% also has 3 sig figs. Don't assume dimensionless means no significant figure rules apply.

Repeated measurements reduce RANDOM error but NOT systematic error — Taking 100 readings averages out random fluctuations, but if your scale is mis-calibrated (systematic error), all 100 readings will be equally wrong.

The mean value is used AS the best estimate of true value — When the true value is unknown, the arithmetic mean of repeated measurements is our best estimate. The error is then calculated relative to this mean.

Least count determines PRECISION, not necessarily ACCURACY — A high-precision screw gauge (LC = 0.001 cm) can give precise but inaccurate readings if zero error is not corrected; accuracy requires both precision and calibration.
practice: The period of oscillation of a pendulum is measured as T = (2.5 \pm 0.1) s and length l = (100 \pm 1) cm. Calculate the percentage error in g = 4\pi²l/T². [Solution: \frac{\Delta g}{g} = \frac{\Delta l}{l} + 2\frac{\Delta T}{T} = \frac{1}{100} + 2\frac{0.1}{2.5} = 0.01 + 0.08 = 0.09 = 9\%. So g = 4\pi²(1.00)/(2.5)² = 6.32 m/s² \pm 9\%.]

The side of a cube is measured as (5.0 \pm 0.1) cm. Find the volume and its percentage error. [Solution: V = s³ = (5.0)³ = 125 cm³. \frac{\Delta V}{V} = 3\frac{\Delta s}{s} = 3 \times \frac{0.1}{5.0} = 0.06 = 6\%. So V = 125 \pm 7.5 cm³ ≈ (125 \pm 8) cm³ (rounded to 2 sig figs in error).]

In an experiment, distance is measured as d = (10.0 \pm 0.2) m and time as t = (2.0 \pm 0.1) s. Find velocity and its maximum percentage error. [Solution: v = d/t = 10.0/2.0 = 5.0 m/s. \frac{\Delta v}{v} = \frac{\Delta d}{d} + \frac{\Delta t}{t} = \frac{0.2}{10.0} + \frac{0.1}{2.0} = 0.02 + 0.05 = 0.07 = 7\%. So v = 5.0 \pm 0.35 m/s ≈ (5.0 \pm 0.4) m/s.]

The resistance R = V/I where V = (100 \pm 5) V and I = (10 \pm 0.5) A. Find R and the maximum percentage error. [Solution: R = 100/10 = 10 \Omega. \frac{\Delta R}{R} = \frac{\Delta V}{V} + \frac{\Delta I}{I} = \frac{5}{100} + \frac{0.5}{10} = 0.05 + 0.05 = 0.10 = 10\%. So R = 10 \pm 1 \Omega.]

A student measures the length of a rod five times: 12.3, 12.5, 12.2, 12.4, 12.6 cm. Find (a) mean length, (b) mean absolute error, (c) percentage error. [Solution: (a) \bar{l} = (12.3+12.5+12.2+12.4+12.6)/5 = 62.0/5 = 12.4 cm. (b) |\Delta l_i|: 0.1, 0.1, 0.2, 0.0, 0.2; \overline{\Delta l} = 0.6/5 = 0.12 cm. (c) Percentage error = (0.12/12.4) × 100 = 0.97% ≈ 1%. Result: l = 12.4 \pm 0.1 cm.]

The density of a material is found by measuring mass m = (5.00 \pm 0.05) kg and volume V = (1.0 \pm 0.1) × 10⁻³ m³. Find the percentage error in density. [Solution: \rho = m/V = 5.00/1.0×10⁻³ = 5000 kg/m³. \frac{\Delta \rho}{\rho} = \frac{\Delta m}{m} + \frac{\Delta V}{V} = \frac{0.05}{5.00} + \frac{0.1}{1.0} = 0.01 + 0.10 = 0.11 = 11\%. So \rho = 5000 \pm 550 kg/m³.]

Two resistors R₁ = (100 \pm 3) \Omega and R₂ = (200 \pm 5) \Omega are connected in series. Find equivalent resistance and its error. [Solution: R_series = R₁ + R₂ = 300 \Omega. \Delta R = \Delta R₁ + \Delta R₂ = 3 + 5 = 8 \Omega. So R = 300 \pm 8 \Omega. Percentage error = (8/300)×100 = 2.67%.]

The radius of a sphere is measured as r = (2.5 \pm 0.1) cm. Find the volume and its absolute error. [Solution: V = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3 = \frac{4}{3}(3.1416)(15.625) = 65.45 cm³. \frac{\Delta V}{V} = 3\frac{\Delta r}{r} = 3 \times \frac{0.1}{2.5} = 0.12. \Delta V = 0.12 × 65.45 = 7.85 ≈ 7.9 cm³. So V = 65.5 \pm 7.9 cm³.]

Express 0.00450600 with the correct number of significant figures if the uncertainty is in the last digit. [Solution: The digits 4, 5, 0, 6, 0, 0 are significant — leading zeros (0.00) are placeholders. Total = 6 significant figures. Scientific notation: 4.50600 × 10⁻³ makes all 6 significant figures explicit.]

A physical quantity P is given by P = a³b²/(\sqrt{c}d). The percentage errors in a, b, c, d are 1%, 2%, 3%, 4% respectively. Find the percentage error in P. [Solution: \frac{\Delta P}{P} = 3\frac{\Delta a}{a} + 2\frac{\Delta b}{b} + \frac{1}{2}\frac{\Delta c}{c} + \frac{\Delta d}{d} = 3(1) + 2(2) + \frac{1}{2}(3) + 4 = 3 + 4 + 1.5 + 4 = 12.5\%.]
universalFacts: The concept of error analysis traces back to Carl Friedrich Gauss (1809) and his work on celestial mechanics — Gauss developed the method of least squares to minimize random errors in astronomical observations, establishing the normal (Gaussian) distribution as the model for random measurement errors.

NEB exam tip: In error propagation problems, always write the formula first, then take logarithms to convert products/powers into sums — log P = 3log a + 2log b - ½log c - log d; differentiating gives \Delta P/P = 3\Delta a/a + 2\Delta b/b + ½\Delta c/c + \Delta d/d. This logarithmic method works for ANY combination of multiplications, divisions, and powers.

The notation \pm in a measurement is NOT a range indicator — When we write 200 \pm 0.2 cm², it means the true value is "about 0.2 cm² away" from 200, not necessarily within [199.8, 200.2]. In rigorous statistics, \pm typically denotes one standard deviation (68% confidence), but in Class 11 NEB, it's treated as the maximum probable error.

Historically, the accuracy of clockmakers determined naval navigation — Before GPS, ships determined longitude using marine chronometers. A time error of just 4 seconds caused a navigational error of ~1 km at the equator. This drove the development of precision measurement and error theory.

The distinction between accuracy and precision comes from metrology — A dartboard analogy: accurate = near bullseye, precise = clustered shots. A medical thermometer might be precise (reproducible to 0.1°C) but inaccurate (off by 2°C due to calibration error). Both qualities matter in science.

In experimental physics, the final answer must always match the precision of the least precise input — If you multiply 2.5 (2 sig figs) by 3.42 (3 sig figs), the result 8.55 must be rounded to 8.6 (2 sig figs). Reporting extra digits falsely implies greater precision than actually exists.

Modern SI units (2019 redefinition) define units via fundamental constants rather than artifacts — The kilogram is now defined by Planck's constant h, the meter by the speed of light c. This eliminates drift in physical prototypes and sets a new standard for measurement accuracy.
